claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: The mRNA decapping process leads to the irreversible removal of the mRNA cap structure, inhibiting translation initiation and inducing XRN1-mediated degradation of mRNA.
claims.source: The mRNA decapping process is crucial for gene regulation because it leads to the irreversible removal of the mRNA cap structure, inhibiting translation initiation and inducing the XRN1-mediated degradation of mRNA through the 5′–3′ mRNA decay pathway (Hsu and Stevens, 1993; Topisirovic et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Decapping is involved in specific mRNA decay pathways, such as AU-rich element-mediated decay, nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), and miRNA-triggered mRNA turnover.
claims.source: Decapping does not only lead to the degradation of bulk mRNA molecules; it is also involved in specific mRNA decay pathways, such as AU-rich element-mediated decay, nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), and miRNA-triggered mRNA turnover (Arribas-Layton et al., 2013; Chen and Shyu, 2003; Fenger-Grøn et al., 2005; Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015; Loh et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: In the context of NMD, target transcripts can be degraded through endonucleolytic cleavage by SMG6.
claims.source: In the context of NMD for instance, target transcripts can be degraded through endonucleolytic cleavage by SMG6 (Eberle et al., 2009; Huntzinger et al., 2008), or be facilitated by SMG5 in conjunction with the NMD effector SMG7 or the decapping factor PNRC2, leading to enhanced deadenylation and decapping (Cho et al., 2009; Fukuhara et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: In eukaryotes, the removal of the mRNA 5′-m7GDP cap structure is catalyzed by the decapping enzyme DCP2, a pyrophosphatase belonging to the Nudix family of proteins.
claims.source: In eukaryotes, the removal of the mRNA 5′-m7GDP cap structure is catalyzed by the decapping enzyme DCP2, a pyrophosphatase belonging to the Nudix family of proteins. This process results in the generation of 5′ monophosphorylated mRNA, which is subsequently targeted for degradation (Arribas-Layton et al., 2013; Lykke-Andersen, 2002; Steiger et al., 2003; van Dijk et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: DCP2 has two major domains: the N-terminal regulatory domain (NRD) and the catalytic Nudix domain.
claims.source: The central component of the complex, DCP2, has two major domains: the N-terminal regulatory domain (NRD) and the catalytic Nudix domain (She et al., 2006; She et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: The positively charged patch of the Nudix domain plays a crucial role in RNA binding.
claims.source: The positively charged patch of the Nudix domain plays a crucial role in RNA binding (Deshmukh et al., 2008; Piccirillo et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: The NRD enhances decapping activity by specifically recognizing the m7G nucleotide of the mRNA cap structure and interacts with the N-terminal EVH1 domain of DCP1.
claims.source: Meanwhile, the NRD enhances decapping activity by specifically recognizing the m7G nucleotide of the mRNA cap structure and interacts with the N-terminal EVH1 domain of the major activator DCP1, further accelerating the decapping process (Chang et al., 2014; Charenton et al., 2016; Dunckley and Parker, 1999; Floor et al., 2010; Mugridge et al., 2016; She et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2002; Wurm et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Yeast Dcp2 has an additional unstructured C-terminal extension that contains short helical leucine-rich motifs (HLMs) responsible for protein–protein interactions.
claims.source: Yeast Dcp2 has an additional unstructured C-terminal extension that contains short helical leucine-rich motifs (HLMs) responsible for protein–protein interactions and elements that inhibit Dcp2 catalytic activity (Charenton et al., 2017; He and Jacobson, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: In contrast to yeast, metazoans have the HLM in DCP1.
claims.source: Interestingly, in contrast to yeast, metazoans have the HLM in DCP1, implying a conserved biological function with evolving regulation of mRNA decapping (Fromm et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claims.claim: DCP2 is capable of demonstrating catalytic activity on its own.
claims.source: While DCP2 is capable of demonstrating catalytic activity on its own (Lykke-Andersen, 2002; van Dijk et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002), it is important to note that additional cofactors are involved in stimulating DCP2 for complete activation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: In yeast, the primary activator of DCP2 is Dcp1, which is essential for decapping activity in vivo.
claims.source: In yeast, the primary activator of DCP2 is Dcp1, which is essential for decapping activity in vivo (Beelman et al., 1996) and considerably enhances the catalytic activity of Dcp2 in vitro (Deshmukh et al., 2008; Floor et al., 2010; She et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Dcp1-dependent decapping mechanisms have been conserved throughout evolution.
claims.source: Localization and functional analysis of decapping proteins across various species indicate that Dcp1-dependent decapping mechanisms have been conserved throughout evolution and play a significant role in the mRNA decapping machinery (Lall et al., 2005; Sakuno et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: The importance of DCP1 in plant species underscores the necessity of the decapping complex for proper plant development.
claims.source: Furthermore, the importance of DCP1 in plant species underscores the necessity of the decapping complex for proper plant development and highlights its potential homology with yeast and human DCP1 (Xu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claims.claim: Proteins such as Edc1-3, Pby1, Lsm1-7, Pat1, and Dhh1 promote decapping by directly or indirectly interacting with Dcp2.
claims.source: In addition to Dcp1, proteins such as Edc1-3, Pby1, Lsm1-7, Pat1, and Dhh1 (PNRC1, PNRC2, EDC3, EDC4, Lsm1-7, Lsm14, PatL1, and DDX6 in metazoans) promote decapping by directly or indirectly interacting with Dcp2 (Charenton et al., 2020; Charenton et al., 2017; Charenton and Graille, 2018; Charenton et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2009; Gaviraghi et al., 2018; He and Jacobson, 2023; He et al., 2022; Jonas and Izaurralde, 2013; Ling et al., 2011; Lobel et al., 2019; Mugridge et al., 2018b).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: High levels of decapping proteins have been detected in large RNP granules, processing bodies (P-bodies), which likely serve as sites for the storage of translationally repressed RNAs and the process of mRNA decay.
claims.source: High levels of these proteins have been detected in large RNP granules, processing bodies (P-bodies), which likely serve as sites for the storage of translationally repressed RNAs and the process of mRNA decay (Eulalio et al., 2007; Jonas and Izaurralde, 2013; Luo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Direct DCP1-DCP2 interactions are weak in metazoans.
claims.source: Although Dcp1 and Dcp2 have been shown to interact strongly in yeast, direct DCP1-DCP2 interactions are weak in metazoans.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge contrasting yeast and metazoans.

claims.claim: The metazoan-specific protein EDC4 functions as a scaffold that brings DCP1 and DCP2 together.
claims.source: Instead, the metazoan-specific protein EDC4, which has binding sites for both DCP1 and DCP2, likely functions as a scaffold that brings these proteins together despite their weak interaction propensity (Chang et al., 2014; Fenger-Grøn et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: DCP1 acts as a binding platform for other coactivator proteins, such as yeast Edc1 and Edc2 and the human PNRC paralogs, PNRC1 and PNRC2.
claims.source: In addition to EDC4, DCP1 acts as a binding platform for other coactivator proteins, such as yeast Edc1 and Edc2 and the human PNRC paralogs, PNRC1 and PNRC2 (Gaviraghi et al., 2018; Jonas and Izaurralde, 2013; Mugridge et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: In metazoans, the HLM domain of DCP1 interacts with the Lsm domains of proteins such as EDC3 and Lsm14 in a mutually exclusive manner.
claims.source: In metazoans, the HLM domain of DCP1 interacts with the Lsm domains of proteins such as EDC3 and Lsm14 in a mutually exclusive manner.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DCP1 interactions.

claims.claim: In multicellular eukaryotes, DCP1 features a C-terminal extension that induces DCP1 trimerization.
claims.source: Moreover, in multicellular eukaryotes, DCP1 features a C-terminal extension that induces DCP1 trimerization, referred to as the trimerization domain (TD). Trimerization is a prerequisite for the incorporation of DCP1 into active decapping complexes and for promoting efficient mRNA decapping in vivo (Fromm et al., 2012; Jonas and Izaurralde, 2013; Tritschler et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: The Lsm domain of Edc3 binds to an extended helix at the C-terminus of the Dcp2 Nudix domain.
claims.source: Recent structural analyses of the Kluyveromyces lactis Dcp1-Dcp2-Edc3 complex indicate that the Lsm domain of Edc3 binds to an extended helix at the C-terminus of the Dcp2 Nudix domain (Charenton et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claims.claim: The activation peptide of Edc1 bridges Dcp1 and Dcp2.
claims.source: Furthermore, the activation peptide of Edc1 bridges Dcp1 and Dcp2, as observed in the Edc1-Dcp1-Dcp2 complex in Saccharomyces pombe and Kluyveromyces lactis (Mugridge et al., 2018b; Wurm et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Edc1 stabilizes Dcp2's catalytically active conformation.
claims.source: These structural insights suggest that Edc1 and Edc3 collaborate through distinct mechanisms, aiding the decapping process (Charenton and Graille, 2018; Charenton et al., 2016; Mugridge et al., 2018a; Mugridge et al., 2018b; Tibble et al., 2021). Specifically, Edc1 stabilizes Dcp2's catalytically active conformation, while Edc3 extends the RNA binding surface of the Dcp2 Nudix domain (Charenton et al., 2016; Mugridge et al., 2018b).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Edc3 extends the RNA binding surface of the Dcp2 Nudix domain.
claims.source: These structural insights suggest that Edc1 and Edc3 collaborate through distinct mechanisms, aiding the decapping process (Charenton and Graille, 2018; Charenton et al., 2016; Mugridge et al., 2018a; Mugridge et al., 2018b; Tibble et al., 2021). Specifically, Edc1 stabilizes Dcp2's catalytically active conformation, while Edc3 extends the RNA binding surface of the Dcp2 Nudix domain (Charenton et al., 2016; Mugridge et al., 2018b).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Structural studies suggest that interactions with Dcp1 are central to the activation of Dcp2.
claims.source: While structural studies suggest that interactions with Dcp1 are central to the activation of Dcp2 (Charenton and Graille, 2018; Deshmukh et al., 2008; Mugridge et al., 2018a; Mugridge et al., 2016; She et al., 2008; Valkov et al., 2016), the lack of structural information on the human decapping complex hinders our understanding of the specific role of human DCP1 in decapping.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: The lack of structural information on the human decapping complex hinders our understanding of the specific role of human DCP1 in decapping.
claims.source: While structural studies suggest that interactions with Dcp1 are central to the activation of Dcp2 (Charenton and Graille, 2018; Deshmukh et al., 2008; Mugridge et al., 2018a; Mugridge et al., 2016; She et al., 2008; Valkov et al., 2016), the lack of structural information on the human decapping complex hinders our understanding of the specific role of human DCP1 in decapping.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claims.claim: Human DCP1a and DCP1b have 31% sequence identity over their entire length.
claims.source: A further complication is the existence of two paralogs of human DCP1, DCP1a, and DCP1b, which have 31% sequence identity over their entire length (Lykke-Andersen, 2002; van Dijk et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Decapping dysfunctions can have detrimental effects on cell growth and have been linked to severe neurological disorders in humans.
claims.source: The fact that decapping dysfunctions can have detrimental effects on cell growth and have been linked to severe neurological disorders in humans (Ahmed et al., 2015; Ng et al., 2015) highlights the importance of understanding the mechanisms of mRNA decapping regulation and the potential therapeutic implications.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claims.claim: Depletion of both DCP1a and DCP1b substantially inhibited SMG7-mediated mRNA degradation, resulting in the accumulation of deadenylated reporter RNA molecules.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we observed that the depletion of both DCP1a and DCP1b substantially inhibited SMG7-mediated mRNA degradation, resulting in the accumulation of deadenylated reporter RNA molecules (Figure 1B, lane 2 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the tethering assay experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: DCP1 knockout led to the substantial accumulation of mRNA decay intermediates when using either Nanos1 or TNRC6A to induce 5′–3′ mRNA decay.
claims.source: To investigate whether the inhibitory effect of DCP1 knockout on decapping is specific to SMG7 or a general effect, we performed tethering assays using either the mRNA decay factor Nanos1 or the crucial miRNA component TNRC6A to induce 5′–3′ mRNA decay. In both cases, DCP1 knockout led to the substantial accumulation of mRNA decay intermediates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), indicating that DCP1 is important for the decapping and degradation of mRNA in general.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the tethering assay experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: DCP1 is important for the decapping and degradation of mRNA in general.
claims.source: To investigate whether the inhibitory effect of DCP1 knockout on decapping is specific to SMG7 or a general effect, we performed tethering assays using either the mRNA decay factor Nanos1 or the crucial miRNA component TNRC6A to induce 5′–3′ mRNA decay. In both cases, DCP1 knockout led to the substantial accumulation of mRNA decay intermediates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), indicating that DCP1 is important for the decapping and degradation of mRNA in general.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tethering assay experiments.

claims.claim: The accumulated RNA fragments had intact 5' caps.
claims.source: The resistance of the transcripts to this treatment is strong evidence that the accumulated RNA fragments had intact 5' caps (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the 5'-phosphate-dependent exonuclease assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: The accumulation of capped mRNA decay intermediates suggests slowed or impaired DCP2-mediated decapping in the absence of DCP1.
claims.source: The accumulation of capped mRNA decay intermediates suggests slowed or impaired DCP2-mediated decapping in the absence of DCP1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Reintroduction of GFP-tagged DCP1a or DCP1b into DCP1a/b-knockout cells led to the restoration of decapping and degradation of the reporter mRNA.
claims.source: To better understand the functional roles of the DCP1 paralogs in decapping, we performed tethering assays and reintroduced GFP-tagged DCP1a or DCP1b into DCP1a/b-knockout cells, leading in both cases to the restoration of decapping and degradation of the reporter mRNA (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the complementation assay shown in Figure 1C and D.

claims.claim: DCP1a and DCP1b are functionally redundant for the general decapping of mRNA.
claims.source: This finding strongly suggests that DCP1a and DCP1b are functionally redundant for the general decapping of mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complementation assay results.

claims.claim: Overexpression of a DCP1a fragment lacking EVH1 domain (ΔEVH1) could not rescue the decapping defect.
claims.source: Strikingly, we observed that overexpression of a DCP1a fragment lacking EVH1 domain (ΔEVH1) could not rescue the decapping defect, indicating that this domain is crucial to coordinate the cellular decapping process.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the domain deletion experiment shown in Figure 1F–H.

claims.claim: The EVH1 domain is crucial to coordinate the cellular decapping process.
claims.source: Strikingly, we observed that overexpression of a DCP1a fragment lacking EVH1 domain (ΔEVH1) could not rescue the decapping defect, indicating that this domain is crucial to coordinate the cellular decapping process.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the domain deletion experiment.

claims.claim: Overexpression of DCP1a without the HLM domain (ΔHLM) partially restored the decapping defect.
claims.source: Overexpression of DCP1a without the HLM domain (ΔHLM) partially restored the decapping defect, indicating a cooperative role for this domain in coordinating DCP1's decapping function.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the domain deletion experiment shown in Figure 1F–H.

claims.claim: The HLM domain has a cooperative role in coordinating DCP1's decapping function.
claims.source: Overexpression of DCP1a without the HLM domain (ΔHLM) partially restored the decapping defect, indicating a cooperative role for this domain in coordinating DCP1's decapping function.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the domain deletion experiment.

claims.claim: All DCP1a constructs containing the EVH1 domain successfully restored the decapping ability of the enzyme complex.
claims.source: Overexpression and subsequent complementation assays in DCP1a/b-knockout cells revealed that all the constructs containing the EVH1 domain successfully restored the decapping ability of the enzyme complex (Figure 1I–K).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the complementation assay shown in Figure 1I–K.

claims.claim: The EVH1 domain of DCP1 is essential for the formation of a functional decapping complex.
claims.source: Together, these findings indicate that the EVH1 domain is of DCP1 is essential for the formation of a functional decapping complex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the domain deletion and complementation experiments.

claims.claim: DCP1 has little involvement in P-body formation.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy analysis of P-body formation indicated that DCP1 has little involvement in P-body formation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence analysis.

claims.claim: In DCP1a/b-knockout cells, DCP2 remained localized in P-body granules.
claims.source: In DCP1a/b-knockout cells, DCP2 remained localized in P-body granules, indicating no correlation between DCP1 and P-body formation or DCP2 localization (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: There is no correlation between DCP1 and P-body formation or DCP2 localization.
claims.source: In DCP1a/b-knockout cells, DCP2 remained localized in P-body granules, indicating no correlation between DCP1 and P-body formation or DCP2 localization (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence analysis.

claims.claim: In DCP1a/b knockout cells, although the number of P-bodies only slightly increased, their size significantly enlarged.
claims.source: Meanwhile, we observed that in DCP1a/b knockout cells, although the number of P-bodies only slightly increased, their size significantly enlarged (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the P-body quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The knockout of DCP1a/b has some impact on the morphology of P-bodies.
claims.source: This suggests that the knockout of DCP1a/b, while not affecting P-body formation, still has some impact on the morphology of P-bodies.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the P-body quantification.

claims.claim: A decrease in the enzymatic activity of DCP2 immunopurified from DCP1a/b knockout cells was observed, but it still retains a considerable decapping ability.
claims.source: We observed a decrease in the enzymatic activity of DCP2 immunopurified from DCP1a/b knockout cells, but it still retains a considerable decapping ability (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vitro decapping assay shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: DCP2 is sufficient for in vitro decapping without DCP1.
claims.source: These data suggest that, in accordance with prior literature, DCP2 is sufficient for in vitro decapping without DCP1 (Lykke-Andersen, 2002; van Dijk et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro decapping assay, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the absence of DCP1, interactions between DCP2 and the decapping factors EDC3, DDX6, and PatL1 were almost completely suppressed.
claims.source: In the absence of DCP1, interactions between DCP2 and the decapping factors EDC3, DDX6, and PatL1 (Edc3, Dhh1, and Pat1 in yeast, respectively) were almost completely suppressed, but not with EDC4 (also known as Ge-1 in Drosophila), a major component of the core decapping complex in metazoans (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the coimmunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The interaction between DCP2 and EDC4 was not suppressed in the absence of DCP1.
claims.source: In the absence of DCP1, interactions between DCP2 and the decapping factors EDC3, DDX6, and PatL1 (Edc3, Dhh1, and Pat1 in yeast, respectively) were almost completely suppressed, but not with EDC4 (also known as Ge-1 in Drosophila), a major component of the core decapping complex in metazoans (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the coimmunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The interaction between DCP2 and PNRC1, as well as PNRC2, was reduced in DCP1a/b-knockout cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, the interaction between DCP2 and PNRC1, as well as PNRC2, which acts in synergy with DCP1 to promote decapping, was reduced in DCP1a/b-knockout cells (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the coimmunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 2F and G.

claims.claim: DCP1 acts as a binding platform for multiple decapping factors and is essential for the interaction of these cofactors with DCP2 in human cells.
claims.source: These findings suggest that DCP1 acts as a binding platform for multiple decapping factors and is essential for the interaction of these cofactors with DCP2 in human cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the coimmunoprecipitation assays.

claims.claim: The EVH1 domain of DCP1a did not interact with any of the decapping factors except for DCP2 and PNRC1/2.
claims.source: The EVH1 domain of DCP1a did not interact with any of the decapping factors except for DCP2 and PNRC1/2 (Figure 3A–D).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the coimmunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 3A–D.

claims.claim: The knockdown of PNRC1 or PNRC2 had only a minor effect on the results of the tethering assays.
claims.source: Unlike the DCP1 knockout, the knockdown of PNRC1 or PNRC2 had only a minor effect on the results of the tethering assays, suggesting that PNRC1 and PNRC2 are not essential for DCP2 activity (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the tethering assay shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: PNRC1 and PNRC2 are not essential for DCP2 activity.
claims.source: Unlike the DCP1 knockout, the knockdown of PNRC1 or PNRC2 had only a minor effect on the results of the tethering assays, suggesting that PNRC1 and PNRC2 are not essential for DCP2 activity (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tethering assay.

claims.claim: The activation of the decapping complex by DCP1a cannot be solely attributed to the binding of decapping factors on the DCP1a scaffold.
claims.source: Therefore, we concluded the activation of the decapping complex by the DCP1a cannot be solely attributed to the binding of decapping factors on the DCP1a scaffold.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PNRC1/2 knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: The mRNA binding affinity of DCP2 is weak in the absence of DCP1 but significantly increases in the presence of DCP1a full-length or the EVH1 domain.
claims.source: Our results show that the mRNA binding affinity of DCP2 is weak in the absence of DCP1 but significantly increases in the presence of DCP1a full-length or the EVH1 domain (Figure 3H and I).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 3H and I.

claims.claim: High levels of DCP2 were observed in the RNA immunoprecipitation assays when the DCP1a EVH1 domain was overexpressed.
claims.source: Reporter RNA was isolated during the decapping process and consistent with the findings of the DCP2 immunoprecipitation assays, high levels of DCP2 were observed in the RNA immunoprecipitation assays when the DCP1a EVH1 domain was overexpressed (Figure 3J).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: DCP1a can regulate DCP2's cellular decapping activity by enhancing DCP2's affinity to RNA.
claims.source: Taken together, we demonstrated that DCP1a can regulate DCP2's cellular decapping activity by enhancing DCP2's affinity to RNA, in addition to bridging the interactions of DCP2 with other decapping factors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA immunoprecipitation assays.

claims.claim: There were significant differences in the transcript profiles of the knockout cells.
claims.source: We performed an RNA-seq analysis of HEK-293T cells lacking DCP1a, DCP1b, or both and compared the results with those from wild-type cells (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D). There were significant differences in the transcript profiles of the knockout cells.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In DCP1a-, DCP1b-, and DCP1a/b-knockout cells, the expression of 604, 1255, and 1146 genes were significantly downregulated, while 504, 677, and 1383 genes were significantly upregulated.
claims.source: In DCP1a-, DCP1b-, and DCP1a/b-knockout cells, the expression of 604, 1255, and 1146 genes were significantly downregulated, while 504, 677, and 1383 genes were significantly upregulated (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: Only a subset of genes dysregulated in both DCP1a- and DCP1b-knockout cells showed alterations in DCP1a/b-knockout cells.
claims.source: Notably, only a subset of genes dysregulated in both DCP1a- and DCP1b-knockout cells showed alterations in DCP1a/b-knockout cells. This observation is further evidence of the crucial role of DCP1 in decapping (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Comparing the transcriptomes of the DCP1a- and DCP1b-knockout cells to the wild type results in many genes that are uniquely altered in DCP1a-knockout or DCP1b knockout.
claims.source: Furthermore, comparing the transcriptomes of the DCP1a- and DCP1b-knockout cells to the wild type results in many genes that are uniquely altered DCP1a-knockout or DCP1b knockout (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that these two proteins regulate distinct sets of genes, whether directly or indirectly.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: DCP1a and DCP1b regulate distinct sets of genes, whether directly or indirectly.
claims.source: Furthermore, comparing the transcriptomes of the DCP1a- and DCP1b-knockout cells to the wild type results in many genes that are uniquely altered DCP1a-knockout or DCP1b knockout (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that these two proteins regulate distinct sets of genes, whether directly or indirectly.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: DCP1a and DCP1b are non-redundant in gene expression regulation.
claims.source: This observation implies that DCP1a and DCP1b are non-redundant in gene expression regulation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: Multiple cancer-related pathways were activated in DCP1a-knockout and/or DCP1b-knockout cells.

results.result: Knockout of both DCP1a and DCP1b substantially inhibits mRNA decapping in vivo, leading to accumulation of capped, deadenylated mRNA intermediates. This effect is general across multiple mRNA decay pathways (SMG7-mediated, Nanos1-mediated, and TNRC6A-mediated), indicating that DCP1 is crucial for mRNA decapping and degradation in human cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 provide converging evidence from multiple tethering assays (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D) showing that DCP1a/b knockout leads to accumulation of capped mRNA decay intermediates across different decay pathways. The 5'-phosphate-dependent exonuclease assay (C47) confirms the cap structure is intact, supporting the conclusion that decapping is impaired. The experiments include appropriate controls (DCP2 E148Q mutant) and test multiple decay factors, strengthening the generality of the finding.

results.result: DCP1a and DCP1b are functionally redundant for general mRNA decapping. Reintroduction of either GFP-tagged DCP1a or DCP1b into DCP1a/b-knockout cells restores decapping and degradation of reporter mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by complementation assays (Figure 1C-D) showing that either paralog can rescue the decapping defect in double knockout cells. This demonstrates functional redundancy for general decapping activity, though the manuscript later shows they have distinct roles in regulating specific endogenous targets.

results.result: The EVH1 domain of DCP1 is essential for cellular mRNA decapping, while the HLM domain plays a cooperative role. Domain deletion experiments show that DCP1a lacking the EVH1 domain cannot rescue decapping defects, whereas deletion of HLM only partially impairs rescue. All constructs containing the EVH1 domain restore decapping ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 are supported by systematic domain deletion and complementation experiments (Figure 1F-K). The experiments show clear functional hierarchy: EVH1 is essential (no rescue without it), HLM is cooperative (partial rescue without it), and TD is dispensable. Multiple constructs were tested, and all containing EVH1 rescued the phenotype, providing strong evidence for this domain's essential role.

results.result: DCP1 has little involvement in P-body formation or DCP2 localization. In DCP1a/b-knockout cells, DCP2 remains localized to P-bodies, and while P-body size increases, their number is only slightly affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 2A-B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C) showing DCP2 colocalization with P-body markers (EDC4, 4E-T, DDX6) in knockout cells. Quantification shows statistically significant increase in P-body size but minimal change in number. This indicates DCP1 is not required for P-body formation or DCP2 recruitment to P-bodies, though it affects P-body morphology.

results.result: DCP2 retains considerable decapping activity in vitro when immunopurified from DCP1a/b knockout cells, though activity is somewhat reduced. This demonstrates that DCP2 is sufficient for in vitro decapping without DCP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by in vitro decapping assays (Figure 2C-D) showing that DCP2 from knockout cells retains decapping activity, though at reduced levels compared to wild-type. This is consistent with prior literature cited. However, the authors appropriately note the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results, emphasizing that in vivo experiments better reflect DCP1's regulatory role in the cellular context.

results.result: DCP1 acts as a binding platform essential for recruiting multiple decapping cofactors to DCP2. In DCP1a/b-knockout cells, interactions between DCP2 and EDC3, DDX6, and PatL1 are almost completely suppressed, while interaction with EDC4 is maintained. Interactions with PNRC1 and PNRC2 are also reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 are supported by coimmunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2E-G) with RNase A treatment to eliminate RNA-mediated interactions. The experiments show differential effects on various cofactors, with EDC4 interaction maintained (consistent with its role as a metazoan-specific scaffold) while other interactions are lost. This provides strong evidence for DCP1's scaffolding function, though the maintained EDC4 interaction suggests additional complexity in the decapping complex architecture.

results.result: The EVH1 domain of DCP1a interacts only with DCP2 and PNRC1/2 among tested decapping factors. However, knockdown of PNRC1 or PNRC2 has only minor effects on decapping, indicating they are not essential for DCP2 activity. This demonstrates that DCP1a-mediated activation cannot be solely attributed to scaffolding of decapping factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by coimmunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3A-D) and PNRC1/2 knockdown tethering assays (Figure 3E-F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The limited interaction profile of the EVH1 domain combined with the minor effect of PNRC1/2 knockdown suggests additional mechanisms beyond scaffolding. This sets up the subsequent investigation of DCP1's role in enhancing DCP2-mRNA binding.

results.result: DCP1 enhances DCP2's mRNA-binding affinity. The mRNA binding affinity of DCP2 is weak in the absence of DCP1 but significantly increases in the presence of DCP1a full-length or the EVH1 domain alone. This represents a key mechanism by which DCP1a regulates DCP2's cellular decapping activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by RNA immunoprecipitation assays using catalytically inactive DCP2 (E148Q) to prevent mRNA degradation (Figure 3H-J). The experiments show increased reporter mRNA association with DCP2 when DCP1a or its EVH1 domain is present. While the authors acknowledge the changes may seem minor in vitro, they appropriately contextualize this within the complex cellular environment where small molecular changes can have amplified effects. The use of inactive DCP2 is a strength, preventing confounding from ongoing decapping.

results.result: DCP1a and DCP1b regulate distinct sets of genes and are non-redundant in gene expression regulation. RNA-seq analysis shows significant differences in transcript profiles between DCP1a-, DCP1b-, and DCP1a/b-knockout cells, with many genes uniquely altered in each single knockout. Only a subset of genes dysregulated in both single knockouts show alterations in the double knockout.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 are supported by comprehensive RNA-seq analysis (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D) with appropriate replication (n=3 biological replicates based on PCA plot). The Venn diagrams and scatter plots clearly show distinct gene expression changes for each knockout. However, the authors appropriately note that these changes could result from both direct effects (target gene accumulation) and indirect effects, which is a limitation. The conclusion of non-redundancy in gene expression regulation is well-supported, though it contrasts with the functional redundancy observed in general decapping assays.

results.result: DCP1a is more strongly associated with cancer than DCP1b. GSEA analysis reveals that multiple cancer-related pathways are activated in DCP1a-knockout cells, including apoptosis, E2F targets, MYC targets, mTOR signaling, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. DCP1a is also involved in embryonic development and cell cycle pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by GSEA analysis (Figure 4C-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H) showing enrichment of cancer-related pathways in DCP1a knockout. The findings are consistent with cited literature on DCP1a's role in embryonic growth and tumor development. However, pathway enrichment analysis has limitations: it shows correlation but not causation, and the enriched pathways could result from indirect effects of gene expression changes. The conclusion about DCP1a being more strongly associated with cancer than DCP1b is reasonable but should be considered preliminary.

results.result: DCP1a and DCP1b have distinct and context-dependent roles in cancer. TCGA analysis shows DCP1a expression is reduced in various cancers and higher DCP1a expression is associated with longer progression-free interval in uterine carcinosarcoma. DCP1b shows variable expression across cancers and has context-dependent associations with survival, suggesting multifaceted roles in tumorigenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C91 are supported by analysis of TCGA data (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C) across multiple cancer types. The survival analyses show statistically significant associations, though effect sizes and confidence intervals should be considered. A limitation is that this is correlative analysis of existing data without experimental validation. The conclusion that DCP1a and DCP1b have distinct targets and non-redundant roles is reasonable but requires further mechanistic investigation. The context-dependent nature of DCP1b's role is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: DCP1a and DCP1b have different effects on cellular metabolism. Metabolomic profiling successfully differentiates DCP1a- and DCP1b-knockout cells. UDP-GlcNAc, GlcNAc, glycerophosphoserine, and glycerophosphocholine levels are elevated in DCP1a- and DCP1a/b-knockout cells, while NAD levels are reduced. DCP1b-knockout cells show elevated LPE(P-18:0).
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 are supported by untargeted metabolomic profiling (Figure 5A-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C) with appropriate technical replication (n=3). PLS-DA shows clear separation of groups, and volcano plots identify significantly altered metabolites. The metabolomic changes are specific to each knockout, supporting distinct metabolic roles. However, the manuscript notes that ~123 metabolites were identified after filtering, which is a relatively small number for untargeted metabolomics. The statistical significance of individual metabolite changes is demonstrated, though the biological significance requires further investigation.

results.result: DCP1a and DCP1b may regulate UDP-GlcNAc and GlcNAc through pathways extending beyond amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism. Integration of transcriptome and metabolome data shows correlation between metabolite levels and transcript levels in the amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism pathway, suggesting intricate and far-reaching roles in cellular metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 integrate transcriptomic and metabolomic data (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), showing correlations between transcript and metabolite levels in the amino sugar pathway. However, the claim that regulation extends "beyond" this pathway is speculative and not directly demonstrated. The correlation between transcript and metabolite levels could be explained entirely within the amino sugar pathway. The conclusion about "intricate and far-reaching roles" is reasonable but requires additional experiments to identify the specific mechanisms and pathways involved. The authors appropriately acknowledge that further studies are necessary.

results.result: The EVH1 domain of DCP1 plays a pivotal role in DCP2 activation. Prior work showed that substituting the conserved NR-loop with a flexible GSSG loop in the EVH1 domain disrupted DCP2 activation without affecting DCP1-DCP2 interaction or integration into decapping factors. Combined with current findings, this demonstrates the EVH1 domain is crucial for coordinating interactions and facilitating conformational changes necessary for efficient mRNA decapping.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 integrate prior published work (Chang et al., 2014) with current findings. The prior study showed that a subtle structural change in the EVH1 domain disrupted DCP2 activation without affecting protein-protein interactions, supporting a role beyond scaffolding. Combined with the current study's findings on EVH1's role in enhancing DCP2-mRNA binding and its essentiality for decapping, this provides strong converging evidence for the EVH1 domain's pivotal role. The integration of prior and current work is appropriate and strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Cell lines deficient in DCP1a, DCP1b, or both were successfully generated using CRISPR/Cas9 in HEK-293T cells. The cells were authenticated and confirmed to be mycoplasma-free.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C108-C110 describe the generation and validation of knockout cell lines. Western blot analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B) and Sanger sequencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) confirm successful knockout. Cell authentication and mycoplasma testing are appropriate quality control measures. The knockout strategy resulted in frameshift mutations leading to premature stop codons in both alleles, which is well-documented.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about mRNA decapping machinery, DCP1, DCP2, and their roles across species. These establish the context and knowledge gaps that motivate the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C43, C104-C105 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. These claims establish: (1) the general importance of mRNA decapping in gene regulation, (2) the roles of DCP1 and DCP2 in yeast and other organisms, (3) the existence of two human DCP1 paralogs with unknown specific functions, and (4) the knowledge gap regarding human DCP1's precise role. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field. These background claims effectively motivate the experimental work.

results.result: DCP1a is a cancer-associated gene whose dysregulation may contribute to cancer onset and progression. DCP1b is also implicated in cancer pathogenesis, though further studies are required to fully understand the roles of both paralogs.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 are conclusions drawn from TCGA analysis and pathway enrichment. While the TCGA data shows altered DCP1a/b expression in cancers and some survival associations, the claim that dysregulation "may play a contributory role" is speculative. The evidence is correlative, not causal. The authors appropriately acknowledge that C107 is speculation and that further studies are required. Without functional validation in cancer models, the cancer-associated role remains uncertain, though the correlative evidence is suggestive.

results.result: DCP1 knockout leads to significant defects in decapping and accumulation of capped, deadenylated mRNA decay intermediates. Tethering assays using SMG7, Nanos1, and TNRC6A showed that depletion of both DCP1a and DCP1b substantially inhibited mRNA degradation, resulting in accumulation of capped mRNA decay intermediates, indicating DCP1 is important for general mRNA decapping and degradation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding as a strength, stating 'Through in vivo tethering assays in CRISPR/Cas9-generated DCP1a/b knockout cells, the authors show that DCP1 depletion leads to significant defects in decapping and the accumulation of capped, deadenylated mRNA decay intermediates.' No concerns were raised about these claims.

results.result: The EVH1 domain of DCP1 is essential for decapping function. Complementation experiments showed that reintroduction of either DCP1a or DCP1b rescued decapping defects, indicating functional redundancy. However, deletion of the EVH1 domain completely abolished rescue ability, while deletion of the HLM domain only partially impaired rescue, demonstrating that the EVH1 domain is crucial for coordinating cellular decapping.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding, noting 'DCP1 truncation experiments reveal that only the EVH1 domain of DCP1 is necessary to rescue decapping defects in DCP1a/b KO cells' as a strength. This is identified as one of the well-supported claims with no concerns raised.

results.result: DCP1 acts as a scaffold for decapping cofactors but these cofactors are not essential for DCP2 activity. Coimmunoprecipitation experiments showed that in the absence of DCP1, interactions between DCP2 and cofactors EDC3, DDX6, and PatL1 were almost completely suppressed, while interaction with EDC4 was maintained. The EVH1 domain only interacted with DCP2 and PNRC1/2. Knockdown of PNRC1 or PNRC2 had only minor effects on decapping, suggesting these cofactors are not essential for DCP2 activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as a strength: 'RNA and protein immunoprecipitation experiments suggest that DCP1 acts as a scaffold to help recruit multiple decapping cofactors to the decapping complex (e.g. EDC3, DDX6, PATL1 PNRC1, and PNRC2), but that none of these cofactors are essential for DCP2-mediated decapping in cells.' No concerns were raised about these findings.

results.result: DCP1 enhances DCP2's mRNA-binding affinity through the EVH1 domain. RNA immunoprecipitation assays showed that mRNA binding affinity of DCP2 is weak in the absence of DCP1 but significantly increases in the presence of DCP1a full-length or the EVH1 domain. The authors conclude that DCP1a can regulate DCP2's cellular decapping activity by enhancing DCP2's affinity to RNA.
results.evaluation: Reviewers identify this as a key weakness, stating this claim 'appears to be at odds with the observations that: (a) in vitro decapping assays with immunoprecipitated DCP2 show that DCP1 knockout does not significantly affect the enzymatic activity of DCP2 (Fig 2C&D)' and '(b) the authors show only weak changes in relative RNA levels immunoprecipitated by DCP2 with versus without DCP1 (~2-3 fold change in Fig 3H).' The reviewer concludes 'there is insufficient evidence here to make a claim that (maybe weakly) enhanced RNA binding induced by DCP1 is what is regulating the cellular decapping activity' and that 'this conclusion is overstated in the revised manuscript.'

results.result: DCP2 retains considerable decapping ability in vitro without DCP1. In vitro decapping assays with immunopurified DCP2 from DCP1a/b knockout cells showed a decrease in enzymatic activity, but DCP2 still retained considerable decapping ability, suggesting DCP2 is sufficient for in vitro decapping without DCP1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note this finding but express concern about its interpretation in relation to the RNA binding claims. The reviewer states 'in vitro decapping assays with immunoprecipitated DCP2 show that DCP1 knockout does not significantly affect the enzymatic activity of DCP2 (Fig 2C&D)' and questions why 'no difference in in vitro decapping activity observed in the absence of DCP1' if DCP1 pivotally regulates decapping through RNA binding enhancement. The reviewer also suggests the kinetic analysis may be missing differences because 'the reaction is basically done in less than 5 minutes under the conditions being assayed.'

results.result: DCP1 has minimal involvement in P-body formation but affects P-body morphology. Immunofluorescence analysis showed that in DCP1a/b-knockout cells, DCP2 remained localized in P-body granules, indicating no correlation between DCP1 and P-body formation or DCP2 localization. However, P-body size significantly enlarged in knockout cells, suggesting some impact on P-body morphology.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these P-body findings. The claims are presented as observational data about localization and morphology, and no critique is offered regarding their validity or interpretation.

results.result: DCP1a and DCP1b regulate distinct sets of genes and have non-redundant roles in gene expression. RNA-seq analysis revealed significant differences in transcript profiles between DCP1a, DCP1b, and double knockout cells, with many genes uniquely altered in each single knockout. Pathway analysis showed activation of multiple cancer-related pathways, with DCP1a more strongly associated with cancer than DCP1b. TCGA database analysis showed DCP1a expression was reduced in various cancers and associated with progression-free interval in certain cancer types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding as a strength: 'The authors investigated the differential roles of DCP1a and DCP1b in gene regulation through transcriptomic and metabolomic analysis and found that these DCP1 paralogs target different mRNA transcripts for decapping and have different roles in cellular metabolism and their apparent links to human cancers.' The reviewer notes they 'can't comment on the experimental details and/or rigor of the transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, as these are outside my expertise,' but does not challenge the conclusions.

results.result: DCP1a and DCP1b have distinct impacts on cellular metabolism. Metabolomic analysis successfully differentiated DCP1a and DCP1b knockout cells, revealing distinct metabolomic profiles. UDP-GlcNAc, GlcNAc, glycerophosphoserine, and glycerophosphocholine levels were elevated in DCP1a and double knockout cells, while NAD levels were reduced. DCP1b knockout cells showed elevated LPE(P-18:0). These metabolite levels correlated with transcript levels in amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism pathways.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding as part of the transcriptomic and metabolomic analysis strength, stating the authors 'found that these DCP1 paralogs target different mRNA transcripts for decapping and have different roles in cellular metabolism.' While noting the analysis is outside their expertise, no concerns are raised about the metabolomic findings.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C44-C48. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers identify the tethering assay evidence for DCP1's role in decapping as a key strength, with accumulation of capped mRNA decay intermediates in knockout cells. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Partial overlap on functional redundancy claims (C49-C50). OpenEval evaluates C49-C50 as supported, while peer review evaluates C49-C50 along with domain deletion claims C51-C56 together as supported. Both agree on the rescue capability but peer review groups this with EVH1 domain findings.

Strong overlap on EVH1 domain essentiality (C51-C56). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers identify the domain deletion experiments showing EVH1's necessity as a key strength. Complete agreement that this finding is well-supported with no concerns.

Perfect agreement on claims C57-C61 regarding P-body localization and morphology. Both evaluations support these observational findings about DCP2 colocalization with P-body markers and effects on P-body size. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Agreement on claims C62-C63 but different interpretations. Both acknowledge the in vitro decapping data showing retained DCP2 activity in knockout cells. OpenEval rates as supported with appropriate contextualization, while peer review rates as uncertain, questioning why in vitro activity is maintained if DCP1 is pivotal for decapping regulation.

Overlap on scaffolding function claims (C64-C67). Both evaluations support the coimmunoprecipitation evidence for DCP1's role in recruiting cofactors. OpenEval focuses on C64-C67, while peer review groups C64-C71 together, both identifying this as a strength.

Overlap on PNRC1/2 interaction claims (C68-C71). OpenEval evaluates these as supported, noting limited EVH1 interaction profile. Peer review groups these with broader scaffolding claims (C64-C71) and supports the finding that cofactors are not essential for decapping.

Major disagreement on RNA binding enhancement claims (C72-C74). OpenEval rates as supported with appropriate contextualization of modest effects. Peer review rates as uncertain, stating the claim is 'overstated' and 'at odds' with in vitro decapping data showing no DCP1 effect, and noting only weak (~2-3 fold) changes in RNA binding.

Overlap on transcriptomic analysis claims (C75-C80). Both evaluations support the RNA-seq findings showing distinct gene expression changes for each paralog knockout. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of methodology, while peer review acknowledges this as a strength despite being outside their expertise.

Overlap on pathway enrichment claims (C81-C84). Both evaluations support the GSEA findings linking DCP1a to cancer-related pathways. OpenEval notes limitations of correlative analysis, while peer review accepts the findings as a strength with caveat about expertise limitations.

Overlap on TCGA analysis claims (C85-C91). Both evaluations support the cancer association findings showing differential roles of DCP1a and DCP1b. OpenEval emphasizes correlative nature requiring validation, while peer review accepts as strength despite expertise limitations.

Strong overlap on metabolomic profiling claims (C92-C96). Both evaluations support the untargeted metabolomics showing distinct metabolic roles for each paralog. OpenEval provides technical assessment, while peer review accepts findings as part of broader transcriptomic/metabolomic analysis strength.

Overlap on integrated transcriptomic/metabolomic claims (C97-C99). OpenEval rates as uncertain, noting speculation about regulation 'beyond' amino sugar pathway. Peer review supports the broader finding of differential metabolic roles but acknowledges expertise limitations in assessing experimental details.
